segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Back when Pete was 18 years old, it was the summer before he went away to college. He's home, in the living room with his dad.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: And he turns to me and he says, Peter, let's go for a drive. And that was not something that he ever said. That's not something that we did.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So Pete knows something's up, but he has no idea what. They go outside, get in the Volvo. Pete asks his dad--

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Shouldn't we get Will, my younger brother? Because he was at home. He was probably 13 or 14. And my dad just shook his head no.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This drive for Pete, alone with his dad, turned out to be kind of a big moment in his life. Before the drive, if he had to describe his family, it wasn't hard. He could do it in two words.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Completely mundane. I mean, we lived outside of DC. My parents worked for the government. I mean, they were good parents. They were kind and attentive. And we would have dinner every night. My dad would cook dinner.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Good cook?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Oh, incredible cook.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The way Pete remembers it, he did salmon Sundays, made a great pot roast, had a pizza that he'd make on Fridays. His mom was the one who'd make sure they did their homework and cleaned their rooms. She was direct and more talkative than their dad, who was really quiet.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: They were not gregarious. They didn't really have friends. They didn't really have hobbies.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, and so now he is in the car with his dad, just the two of them. Dad pulls out of the driveway.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: So we start driving through our neighborhood, and we get to the stoplight at the end of our neighborhood. And he says to me, Peter, it's time to tell you about the family business, espionage. I mean, my first reaction was, like, what are you doing right now? What kind of joke is this?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: And then the next thing that he said is, open the glove box. And so I opened the glove box, and inside was a sheet of paper. And he said, take out that sheet of paper. And so I took it out, and I'm scanning the page, and it's his resume from the CIA.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Did you know he worked for the CIA?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Where did you think he worked?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Well, he said he worked at the State Department.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But now, on this sheet of paper, it listed all the different countries that Pete had lived with his parents-- Germany and the Netherlands and Jamaica, countries where Pete had always thought that his dad was going off to an embassy or consulate every day to work for the State Department.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: And I'm seeing, like, counterintelligence, and counterinsurgency, and deputy chief, chief of station, case officer. I didn't know what to ask next. And I honestly don't know that we talked very much at all. So we actually drove in a big loop and drove back down into the driveway. And I was like, oh, wait, does Mom know about this? And my dad goes, oh, um, she works there, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This stunned him. His dad, he could kind of see. His dad was quiet, like somebody who keeps keep secrets.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: But with my mom, it was completely out of-- it was just a complete surprise because of how she was.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: She just was somebody who-- it just seemed like you were getting exactly what you got. She just didn't really seem like somebody who could deceive. But I guess she was.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And were they the kind of CIA employees who analyze data and sit at a desk, work a desk? Or were they out in the field, spying, pretending to be people who they aren't, carrying a gun? Were that kind of CIA?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: They were out in the field. Yeah, they were undercover. They had passports with other names. And the way it was described to me is that they were not spies. They were recruiting spies from other countries. And in doing so, they were pretending to be people who they were not.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Pete says before this, he just hadn't really thought much about his parents and their lives and their jobs. He was a kid. He once asked his mom, what do you actually do at your government job all day long?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: And I think my mom said something like, oh, it's just meetings and memos. And I was like, yeah, I figured. Just boring stuff.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. Which, I have to say, I bet there were meetings and memos, so it's like, that isn't 100% lie. It's just leaving some stuff out.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Yeah. No, definitely using boringness as a kind of deception.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In retrospect, Pete says, there were clues that he could have maybe picked up on. His mom spoke several languages. The family lived most of his life in other countries. His dad owned a 9 millimeter pistol and was always up at 4:00 in the morning to go running on a track. It was the fact that his parents didn't have friends and never had anybody over to the house-- which, of course, doesn't mean that you're a spy, but still.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Yeah, it actually wasn't until a lot later that I realized that a lot of adults do have friends and still hang out. And there were things like when I would go to the mall with my mom, she always made sure we knew a code word. And she would say like, OK, so if Mommy's ever not here, and somebody comes to pick you up, make sure they know the code word. And the code word was always "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, anytime you would go to the mall, your mom would remind you of this?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Yeah, we'd be in the back seat, and she'd be like, OK, boys, what's the code word? And we'd say, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: At the time, he says, he chalked it up to 1990s stranger danger stuff, but he learned that other parents do not do this. And he told me there was one more clue about his parents' jobs, a clue was sitting right there during the years they moved back to Virginia.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Maybe the biggest clue of all is that we lived right across the street from the CIA headquarters.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, what?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Yeah. [LAUGHS] That makes a lot of sense because my dad was super pragmatic, and he hated traffic.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: To be clear, they weren't literally across the street, but in a neighborhood right across the street. Door to door, less than five minutes. Pete's parents are both dead now. They both retired from the CIA after long careers-- which is why it's OK to talk about it here on the radio, by the way. But when Pete learned about this, it really did make their lives seem so much more impressive.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Like, they met in the CIA, fell in love in the CIA. They were globetrotting and bringing their kids around and doing God knows what.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm not exactly sure how to ask this question, so I'm just going to ask this straight out. Like, the one thing that I know about spies from movies is that they're all really, really hot. Were your parents really hot?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: [CHUCKLING] I mean, yeah, they were hot. Yeah, they were hot. They were very attractive people. My mom was-- I have these old pictures of her, and she's just beautiful.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And your dad?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Yeah, handsome guy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's this concept that originally was in video games, and then it spread to TV shows and to social media, where-- OK, say, in a video game, there's the universe that everything takes place in, right? And then at some point, the game creators do a new lore drop, where they give backstory or reveal important details that suddenly make everything seem different and richer and more complicated, shed a whole new light.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Pete had that. He had a new lore drop in his actual life. He thought his parents were one thing, then learned backstory that changed his whole picture of them. So what's that like to live through in real life?

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, I think at first, it was a shock, the fact that they were able to deceive me for my whole life. And that is just weird. It did make me look at them differently. Like, wow, the rug just got pulled from under me. Everything I know is a lie. But then when that wears off, it's kind of like, well, it's still just Mom and Dad.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Pete says everybody goes through the thing when they grow up, where they learn to see their parents not just as the boring human furniture around the house of their childhood. And for most of us, the new information that we absorb about our parents happens over years. The new lore drop version that Pete got was just kind of the accelerated program.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: Yeah, I got it all in one drive.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our show, we have other human beings who are not video game characters, and they're not fictional people on long-running television series, who get hit with all new information about their own lives, backstories that rewrite everything, new lore drops in real life. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. Today on the show, I will still be playing the part that I always play here. And I have not learned that I am a princess from Genovia, and my grandmother is actually Julie Andrews. I am still Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. Act One, Save the Drama for Your Grandmama. Sometimes, a lore drop happens when you least expect it, like in this next story. Aviva DeKornfeld explains.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: When I first met Jake, it was obvious. This is a guy who was hardwired to try and connect with people. He's like this friendly bulldozer, Kool-Aid Man-ing his way into emotional intimacy. And Jake's always been this way, in part, perhaps, because he grew up surrounded by people. He comes from this big Irish Catholic family in Rhode Island, and he had a sort of sitcom upbringing. His aunts and uncles and cousins all lived close by. One grandma lived literally next door. The other set of grandparents lived a 15-minute walk from his house, and Jake saw them every day. It was the best.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And then, when he was seven years old, his family moved to Vermont, away from his extended family. And he hated it, really missed them. And this missing only intensified when his grandma back in Rhode Island was diagnosed with breast cancer. To little Jake, it was obvious what to do.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: I just started calling her all the time, and I think because I just wanted to keep talking to her because I was so afraid she was going to die.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Oh, my God. It's so sweet.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: I know. [LAUGHS] And it's funny to think back on because it was so purely intentioned, but it's also so-- the motives of it are so transparent that it must have just been a reminder to my grandmother every day, like, this kid thinks you're going to die because you might. You know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: It was kind of like no--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: She was like, OK, relax.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: No, 'cause she was like, I was trying to have one day of fucking peace. And I'm like, hi, Grandma, can I talk to you again before you die?

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: I kind of have this memory of the calls kind of running out of steam a little bit because I was calling every single day, and I was like eight or nine. And so it's like, what? What do you have to talk about, you know? And so I think I had introduced her to Harry Potter, just as I had started reading it. And I think we were then-- we would read them at the same time, and we would read a chapter a night, talk on the phone the next day. We would discuss the chapter, sort of like book club with my grandma.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: I remember-- my mom always jokes one of the most upset times she ever saw me was I caught that my grandma had read ahead. Because she accidentally said something on one of the calls that hadn't happened yet. And I was like, what are you talking about? And she was like, well, doesn't it? And I was like, you read ahead. And she had read the whole book because she couldn't put it down because she loved it.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: But I was like, never do that again. Swear to me that you'll never-- because I loved that I had that experience with her.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: This Harry Potter book club evolved into talking about other books, books they were reading separately. The way it worked, they would each read their own book, and then they'd hop on the phone and summarize it for the other person, chapter by chapter.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: It was part of my nightly ritual. I feel like it was come home, do homework, maybe have dinner, then call Grandma, and recap the book. Because I always loved recapping my book to her. I loved having someone to tell this story to so that it was like, I loved being able to retell it. I want to tell her this story in the way it made me feel. I want to make sure I hide this suspense. I want to-- if there was a surprise in the book, I wanted to make sure I tell her the story of the book in a way that keeps the surprise, so that she's as surprised when I tell her as I was when I read it. And then I'd be like, OK, what about your books? And she would tell me.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: And I remember kind of clocking pretty early on that she definitely didn't have that same flair for-- she just didn't-- she would be like, oh, and then, yeah, they're starting to fall in love. And I'd be like, well, how do they fall in love? Why do they like each other? I felt very connected to her through the books and through the storytelling.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Because I think my grandma was not-- she wasn't particularly forthcoming about herself. She wasn't someone who would come home and drop her bag and like, God, I gotta tell you about my day. That was not her. And this was the first time that I felt like I was having a conversation with an adult who was talking to me about stuff going on in their own life, even if it was just the book they were reading.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Jake's grandma worked at Filene's, in the shoe department. She was a real coupon hound, loved a sale. She was nice, but not exactly sweet in a grandmotherly kind of way. She was often way too honest. Like, if you said you weren't feeling good about yourself because your clothes didn't fit right, she would offer, well, you gained weight.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: She liked reading all kinds of books, but she especially loved thrillers. Jake remembers one of her books in particular, Smoke and Mirrors, about a librarian whose half-sister was murdered. The librarian tries to figure out who murdered her half-sister with the help of a guy who knew her. It was suspenseful. His grandma loved a mystery.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The two kept this book club going for years. Jake would pace back and forth in the hall between the dining room and living room in his house in Vermont, phone tucked under his ear, while his grandma sat nestled in her favorite armchair back in Rhode Island. The calls were long, sometimes lasting hours.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Jake says his summaries were, unsurprisingly, pretty exhaustive. He didn't want to leave a single detail out, until, when he was 12 or so, he stopped being completely honest with his grandma about what he was reading because he started feeling like there was something off about the books he liked. He worried they were too girly.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: The ones where I was like, oh, these were the ones that really caused a crisis for me, there was this series of books called Twitches, which were about twin witches. [LAUGHS] And they were like-- the covers were like those old-school, early 2000s photoshoots where they would do stock image photoshoots. It wasn't like an illustration. It was like a photoshoot of two teenage girls.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Like Olson twins style.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Totally.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Matching outfits.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Exactly. Yeah, yeah, yeah. It was about these two girls who found out that they were adopted and that they were twins. They're also witches. When they meet, they develop magical powers. And I was like, well, I literally have to read these. But I don't want to tell my grandma that I'm reading a book about two teenage girls that have magical powers and like boys. And also, I don't want to carry this book around at school. And so I think that's when I started editing a little bit and--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And why didn't you want your grandma to know you were reading those books?

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Because I think I knew it was speaking to something. I think I was also probably starting to realize-- because I also was a pretty effeminate child. So at this point, I was already getting called gay. So I think this was all kind of interwoven.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And so do you remember intentionally deciding to start changing details?

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: I remember in Twitches, I think I changed their gender. I think I made them both boys. I think I changed their powers. I think I said that one could move things with their mind and that one was strong.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And the details you were changing, it was to make it align with what you thought a straight boy would be reading?

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: I guess so. I was like, I'll change these details because they don't affect the plot. And so I was like, I'm not going to change the plot. I'm just going to change the details around it to make it a little bit more masc. So it's going to be-- instead of being able to passively stop it through clairvoyance and telepathy, it's like, they use their physical powers of telekinesis and strength.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And do you think you were convincing? Do you think that she thought that you were straight at the time?

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: No. I don't think that anyone ever thought I was straight.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: No, I don't think so.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: It's really sweet and really sad to imagine you putting on this disguise by changing the details for your grandma. It's like you're wearing a fake mustache, but it's actually askew, and you have no idea. And everyone's like, that's not a real mustache.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Yeah, 100%. And as though like if I'd been sitting here talking to you for an hour and a half, and then just suddenly put the mustache on and expect you to think it was real. You've been talking--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: --to me without a mustache this whole time. And I also think this kind of led to the end of the book club a little bit, was when I started to be like, I don't want to read these books and have to tell my grandma. But you know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Also, she beat the cancer. Congratulations. So I was less scared about her dying.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Oh, so you were like, OK, it's not an emergency.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: I think kind of. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: It took Jake a few more years to formally come out to his family. He was 16. And he told me, he thinks he remembers his grandma mentioning his coming out once and saying that she loved him. But it was such a non-issue that he can't even really remember specifics. Jake's sexuality, that is not the lore drop in this story. There was one, but it came years later, when Jake was in his 30s. By then, his grandma had developed dementia and then got really sick. Jake made a point to visit her every month or two. And then one day--

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: I was visiting my grandma, and she was in in-home hospice. And it was kind of sad. And she was on the first floor in the living room. And then I went up to my mom's old bedroom. And my mom's bedroom, there's this radiator that always was just covered in my grandma's books. And I remember being in-- I think I probably went up to the room to take a breather or something. And I remember seeing the books on the windowsill and on the radiator.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: He saw titles he remembered from when he was a kid, the book she'd recapped for him.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: And I remember I picked up one of the books and thumbed through it and found a sex scene. And I was like, was she reading-- they're romance novels. These were sexy books. And so I picked them up, and I started flipping through them. And I just remember it being graphic in the way that it described genitals. It wasn't just like, and then we went to the bedroom. It was like, [BLEEP]. You know what I mean? It was like that. And I was like, oh, oh, OK. I was like, are those all smut?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yes, Jake's grandma was an avid reader of smut. Jake sat there laughing out loud to himself as he started googling his grandma's favorite authors-- Jayne Ann Krentz, who wrote the book Grand Passion, in which protagonist Max Fortune heads to a B&B in search of his hidden inheritance, only to find himself irresistibly compelled by the attractive innkeeper, Cleopatra.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: JD Robb-- she wrote the book Naked in Death, where a woman somehow works through her past trauma by sleeping with a hot and mysterious Irish businessman. And another one from Jayne Ann Krentz that Jake remembered his grandma recapping to him, Smoke and Mirrors, the one about the librarian traveling around trying to solve her half-sister's murder with the help of a guy she meets along the way. That was the way Jake remembered it, anyway. But now, reading the book--

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: The whole book is just her wanting to have sex with this man. That's the entire book. The murder is almost never mentioned. They're just walking around this town, trying to find out if the murder-- the entire time, she's just like, this man is so hot. She literally had to make up so much plot. This is so central to the plot. I remember thinking, like, damn, Grandma doesn't give that much of a shit about the narrative. And I'm like, no, Grandma was making up a narrative because half of the plot was about these people having sex. So you want me to read this passage?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: OK. In this part of the book, they just tried to break into a house to look for clues. And an unseen person chased them out of the house, and they had to run away. And now, they're back at his place, and they're safe. OK.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: "Thomas shrugged out of his jacket and came to stand behind her. Their eyes met in the mirror. Unlike her, he looked terrific, she thought, hard, tough, and totally in control. She had to fight an irresistible urge to turn and put her head into his chest. His hands closed over her shoulders. 'Take it easy. You're just feeling the aftershock of the adrenaline. It'll fade.' 'I know.'

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: The weight of his hands was not having the calming, soothing effect he probably intended. She suddenly wanted to do a lot more than just put her head down on his shoulder. She looked at his mouth in the mirror and wondered what would it be like to kiss him, wondered how his mouth would feel on other parts of her body." [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Let's stop there, because we can't conjure an image on the radio.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: You guys were doing the same thing.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: We were doing the same thing.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: What went through your head when you realized that?

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: It really tickled me. I was like-- because I remembered that feeling of being so afraid towards the end of the time when we were calling each other, that I would out myself, or just feeling-- once I became a sexual person myself or pubescent myself, those conversations about those books being like, ah! Don't see me!

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: And realizing she probably felt a version of that the whole time.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Totally.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Or it was just having to constantly think about, OK, don't talk about when they had sex in the kitchen. But what happened to the plotline? I don't know. It makes me feel closer to her that we were doing this song and dance.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: I love the idea that you and your grandma were lying to one another three times a week in the name of bonding.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Exactly. It's like, "lie" almost feels like too harsh of a word. Do you know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: It's just like two people translating what's going on in their lives for the other person, you know?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Right, it's a version of what we all do all the time.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: 100%, you know? When we talk to our parents about our relationship, you might not be like, well, I think I might break up with him because the sex is not great. Like, you might-- ah, I'm just not feeling it. You know what I mean? We do these edits all the time, you know?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah, like, yeah, we were fighting, and then we made up.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Yeah. [LAUGHS] Exactly.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Jake's grandma died this past June. She was 84. Jake and his grandma and their book club, it was never really about the books, obviously. The point was to spend time with one another, to feel close. And it worked. It worked so well that Jake still gets to spend time with her, even now, even in some very unexpected moments.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: I've been watching Heated Rivalry, which is this HBO Max show that's based on a romance novel, but it's a gay romance novel. It's about hockey players. And I'm loving it. It's my favorite show right now. And I'm kind of laughing to myself as I watch it because I'm like, I come from a line of people who enjoy this. This is like-- you know? It's like--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: I'm continuing my family tradition.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Not that I'm think-- let's be clear to the listener. I'm not thinking about my grandma, necessarily, when I'm watching a lot of those scenes. But when I think about it now, I'm like, there is something kind of nice about that, I guess. I found my version of it that I enjoy. There was a period of time in my life where I was terrified of my grandma knowing I was gay, and now I'm watching gay smut on HBO. And I'm like, the gene that makes me like this comes from her.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Sometimes the new lore drop isn't some big revelation. Sometimes it's just a funny little detail. You get to enjoy it and carry on with your day.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Aviva DeKornfeld is one of the producers of our show. Jake is a comedian. He told a version of this story on stage, which is where we first heard about it.
